summary: Bharat Coking Coal mines coal and sells it to steel-related and other industrial customers. Some coal is washed before sale to make it more suitable for the buyer.
description: Coal is taken out of mines, prepared and moved to customers. Some suitable coal is used to make coke, a processed form of coal used to make iron for steel. That is why this business is connected to steel-making as well as to coal used as fuel.
money: Customers pay for the coal or other saleable products they receive. The company must cover mine workers, contractors, machines, fuel, washing, transport arrangements and other costs. It also has to pay for developing mines and meeting land and environmental obligations.
customers: Steel-related buyers purchase suitable coking coal, while power and other industrial customers buy products suited to their needs. The buyer pays for a specified quantity and quality; every load of coal is not equally useful or equally valuable.
drivers: How much usable coal can be mined and sold, its quality, the agreed selling price, washing results, transport availability and the cost of keeping mines operating safely.

groups.title: Coal for the steel-making chain
groups.explanation: Coking coal is coal with properties suitable for making coke for iron production. A buyer’s quality requirements matter: another type of coal sold mainly as fuel may not be a substitute.

groups.title: Coal cleaned before sale
groups.explanation: A washery is a plant that separates coal from some unwanted material. The buyer receives a product better suited to its requirements. Not all the material entering the plant becomes the same clean-coal product.

groups.title: Coal for other fuel uses
groups.examples: Non-coking coal for power and industrial customers.
groups.explanation: These buyers need coal for their own fuel requirements. The quantity, quality and agreed price can differ from the coal bought for making coke.

groups.title: Other material from washing
groups.examples: Middlings, slurry, rejects and other washery outputs.
groups.explanation: Washing separates the incoming material into different outputs. Middlings are lower-quality mixed material; slurry contains fine material mixed with water. What can be sold or needs suitable handling affects the cost of running the washery.

basics.title: Quality matters as much as weight
basics.text: Coal contains different amounts of useful fuel and material that becomes ash when burned. Grade is the company’s quality classification. Customers pay under the agreed quality and pricing terms, not just for a truck’s weight.

basics.title: Mined, delivered and paid for are different stages
basics.text: Production means coal taken out through operations. Offtake means coal sent out to customers on the company’s stated basis. If transport is delayed, the company may produce coal but keep it in stock rather than sell and collect payment for it.

steps.title: Prepare the mine and extract coal
steps.text: Arrange access, workers and machines. Where needed, remove earth and rock above the coal before mining it.

steps.title: Prepare the customer’s product
steps.text: Sort, size or wash coal as required. Check the amount and quality of the usable products obtained.

steps.title: Load and send the coal
steps.text: Arrange road or rail movement and complete the agreed quantity and quality checks.

steps.title: Bill the buyer and collect
steps.text: Charge for the sale under its terms and receive payment. Meanwhile, wages, contractors and mine-development work still need funding.

specifics.title: A bigger washery does not guarantee more clean coal
specifics.text: Capacity is how much raw material a plant can process. Recovery, also called yield, is how much of the desired product comes out. Incoming quality, breakdowns and demand affect what the plant can sell.

specifics.title: Mining costs begin before coal is sold
specifics.text: The company may spend on machinery, mine access and removing earth before it can produce coal. It also faces costs for restoring land and closing mines later. Those obligations are part of the business, even when payment comes in a different year.

specifics.title: Opening a plant is only the start
specifics.text: The official Bhojudih disclosure records the washery starting commercial operations. The following test is practical: does raw coal arrive, does the plant run reliably, and will customers buy its output?

watch: Is mined coal reaching paying customers?
Unsold coal does not pay the next wage or contractor bill.

Compare production with deliveries to customers and coal left in stock. Look for transport delays, weather and mine conditions that explain a gap; do not assume all new production has already been sold.
Does washing produce enough usable coal?
The incoming load and clean-coal output are different quantities.

Read the amount processed, usable output, by-products and operating costs. Ask whether a new washery runs reliably and has buyers for its products rather than relying on its advertised capacity alone.
Why is the price received changing?
A different quality or type of sale can change the average price.
Read coal grades, buyer agreements, quality disputes and selling-price commentary. Separate a higher price from selling more coal; they can affect the business differently.
Can the mines pay for today’s work and future obligations?
Equipment, workers and restoring mined land all require money.

Read day-to-day cash generation with spending on mines, machines and removing overlying earth. Check provisions, which are estimated future obligations recorded in the accounts, and when the actual payments are expected.
What could stop mining or delivery?
Safety, environmental permissions and transport can limit sales.

Use the company’s disclosures to identify the affected mine or route, the problem and what is being done. Check whether it is a local delay or something that affects a wider part of the company’s work.
risks: Weather, unsafe conditions, machine failures or other incidents can reduce output.
Coal quality is poorer than expected
More unwanted material or weak washing results can reduce the useful product or price received.
Industrial demand, rail availability and road movement can hold up deliveries and payment.
Land and environmental work costs money
Permissions, restoration and mine closure may require spending beyond the immediate cost of extraction.
context: Think of the whole route from mine to buyer

A mine needs more than coal underground. Workers must extract it, the right product must be prepared, transport must be available and a buyer must pay. Finding which stage is holding up that route is more useful than reading production alone.
quiz: If a washery can process more raw coal, must sales of clean coal rise by the same amount?
No. Some input becomes other products or unwanted material, and the plant still needs reliable operation, customer demand and transport.
sources: Official financial-result notes and business scope

financialNotes.title: Keep coal prices and quantities separate
financialNotes.text: Use the audited annual revenue and profit together with the stated reporting scope and accounting cautions. Coal output, dispatches and realised selling prices help explain the business but do not establish separate profit for each coal grade or customer. Read levy, tax and balance-reconciliation notes before treating reported profit as cash available for distribution.

financialNotes.title: Check the reporting boundary
financialNotes.text: The cited result notes describe coal mining and related services without separate reportable segments. Do not create a profit allocation between raw coal, washed coal and individual mines from sales or output proportions.
